channel.title: NYT Book Reviews (Filtered)
channel.description: Actual book reviews from the New York Times, filtered from the noisy Books RSS feed.

item.title: “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” by Charles Spencer
item.description: “Swan Song,” Charles Spencer’s memoir of Lady Diana, is full of love and vengeance.
item.author: Alexandra Jacobs

item.title: ‘Anti-Zionism,’ by Benjamin Moser
item.description: In a new book, the prizewinning biographer Benjamin Moser charts a tradition of Jewish opposition to Zionism and recounts his belated conversion to that view.
item.author: Michael S. Roth

item.title: ‘The Age of Cures,’ by Barry Werth
item.description: In “The Age of Cures,” the journalist Barry Werth shows how American drug manufacturers got big and then came under attack.
item.author: Nicola Twilley

item.title: ‘Said the Dead,’ by Doireann Ni Ghriofa
item.description: Doireann Ni Ghriofa’s “Said the Dead” is a fusion of biography, memoir and poetry drawn from century-old casebooks.
item.author: Idra Novey

item.title: ‘Shadow Before the Flame,’ by Catherine Grace Katz
item.description: In “Shadow Before the Flame,” Catherine Grace Katz puts us back on the famously doomed airship.
item.author: Keith O’Brien

item.title: ‘Crossing the Red Line,’ by Akbar Shahid Ahmed
item.description: In “Crossing the Red Line,” Akbar Shahid Ahmed goes behind the scenes in the Biden White House in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks.
item.author: Peter Beinart

item.title: ‘Roll the Calls,’ by Ari Emanuel
item.description: Fights, feuds and insults are all in a day’s work for Ari Emanuel, who offers an unvarnished look at his rapacious career in a new memoir.
item.author: Alexandra Jacobs

item.title: ‘Hollywood, Ending,’ by John Green
item.description: In John Green’s “Hollywood, Ending,” two young actors navigate the highs and lows of Hollywood.
item.author: David Canfield

item.title: ‘Ausländer,’ by Michael Moritz
item.description: In “Ausländer,” Michael Moritz, the managing partner of a venture capital firm, examines his inheritance.
item.author: Julian Borger

item.title: ‘The Rouse,’ by China Miéville
item.description: “The Rouse,” by China Miéville, is a decade-spanning epic about a secret military unit trying to raise and weaponize the dead.
item.author: Jeff VanderMeer

item.title: ‘When America Roared,’ by Jonathan Kaufman
item.description: In “When America Roared,” Jonathan Kaufman draws together a bushel of figures who thrived in one fateful decade.
item.author: Rick Perlstein

item.title: ‘True North,’ by Paul Theroux
item.description: In “True North,” the veteran travel writer Paul Theroux crisscrosses the country of his forebears for insights about how it differs from his own.
item.author: Jennifer Szalai

item.title: ‘Live Laugh Love,’ by Kristin Kobes Du Mez
item.description: In “Live Laugh Love,” Kristin Kobes Du Mez examines how Christian women absorbed the idea that material abundance was evidence of divine favor.
item.author: Caroline Fraser

item.title: ‘Our Noble Selves,’ by Kate Atkinson
item.description: “Our Noble Selves” takes place amid the 1951 Festival of Britain, when a traumatized ex-war reporter and P.O.W. goes from government cog to murder suspect.
item.author: Sadie Stein

item.title: ‘End Times Fascism,’ by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor
item.description: In “End Times Fascism,” Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that apocalyptic ideology has taken hold over American elites.
item.author: Damon Linker

item.title: ‘Fallow,’ by Sarah Anderson
item.description: In Sarah Anderson’s satirical novel, “Fallow,” a debt-laden woman becomes a professional surrogate for a corporate behemoth.
item.author: Hilary Leichter

item.title: ‘The Newer World,’ by Sebastian Barry
item.description: Sebastian Barry’s new novel tours a post-Civil War America where cruelty is ever-present but love endures.
item.author: Ian McGuire

item.title: ‘Corner Boy’ and ‘Gonzo Neurotic’
item.description: Two career-spanning essay collections, from Nik Cohn and Jerry Stahl, revel in life’s margins and recapture auras past.
item.author: Dwight Garner

item.title: ‘Profiles in Cowardice,’ by Jacob Weisberg
item.description: In “Profiles in Cowardice,” Jacob Weisberg offers a grim twist on John F. Kennedy’s collection of heroic biographies.
item.author: Joseph O’Neill

item.title: ‘Exit Party,’ by Emily St. John Mandel
item.description: In “Exit Party,” by Emily St. John Mandel, two versions of America’s future crash into each other.
item.author: Lincoln Michel

item.title: ‘Redwood,’ Ben Macintyre
item.description: In “Redwood,” Ben Macintyre tells the story of a Russian spy in Iran who betrayed his country in exchange for an unusual request.
item.author: Joseph Finder

item.title: ‘A Shadow Over the World,’ by William I. Hitchcock
item.description: In “A Shadow Over the World,” William I. Hitchcock shows how the early struggle against totalitarianism was rife with contradictions.
item.author: Kevin Peraino

item.title: ‘Mind vs. Machine: The Chess Match That Changed the World,’ by Maurice Ashley and Steve Sheinkin
item.description: A new book takes kids whose phones can beat grandmasters back to a 1997 nail-biter.
item.author: John Schwartz

item.title: ‘Dressing the Queen,’ by Kate Strasdin
item.description: In a new book, the fashion historian Kate Strasdin looks at the makers who designed the monarch’s sartorial persona.
item.author: Caroline Weber

item.title: ‘Mock Heart,’ by Jill Bialosky
item.description: The new and selected poems in Jill Bialosky’s “Mock Heart” show her steadily circling desire and domesticity.
item.author: Carol Muske-Dukes

item.title: ‘Call It Evil,’ by Susan Neiman
item.description: In a new book, Susan Neiman argues that by defining evil in terms of individual monstrousness we fail to perceive its widespread hold on our culture.
item.author: Jennifer Szalai

item.title: ‘Is This It,’ by Steven Hyden
item.description: Steven Hyden considers the cultural shifts of the past 25 years in a new book about the band.
item.author: Peter C. Baker

item.title: ‘Money to Burn,’ by William D. Cohan
item.description: In “Money to Burn,” William D. Cohan charts the rise and fall of the Wall Street billionaire Leon Black.
item.author: Jonathan Mahler

item.title: ‘The Pirate Queen,’ by Ariel Lawhon
item.description: In a new novel, the author Ariel Lawhon revives a 16th-century sea captain previously pushed to the margins.
item.author: S. Kirk Walsh

item.title: ‘Taipei Story,’ by R.F. Kuang
item.description: “Taipei Story,” R.F. Kuang’s seventh book in eight years, is about an American student in Taiwan.
item.author: Lauren Christensen

item.title: ‘Living With Freddie,’ by Anna Heyward
item.description: In “Living With Freddie,” Anna Heyward recalls the pet who taught her “to be human.”
item.author: John Williams

item.title: ‘Switzy,’ by Emma Cline
item.description: In an impressive change of pace, Emma Cline’s new novel gets inside the head of a stoic businessman with dementia.
item.author: Alexandra Jacobs

item.title: ‘Tower Hill,’ by Alan Taylor
item.description: In “Tower Hill,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning scholar Alan Taylor pulls apart the twisted logic of a Virginia slave owner and his descendants.
item.author: Richard Kreitner

item.title: ‘All the Presidents’ Wars,’ by Peter Bergen
item.description: In “All the Presidents’ Wars,” the journalist Peter Bergen traces the many missteps of U.S. military action in the Middle East.
item.author: Scott Anderson

item.title: ‘The Living Realm,’ by Jordan Tannahill
item.description: In “The Living Realm,” an expat in Germany is visited by phantoms.
item.author: Christopher Bollen

item.title: ‘The Ghost of the Mountains,’ by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi
item.description: In “The Ghost of the Mountains,” Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi proves there is no substitute for old-fashioned field study.
item.author: Miriam Horn

item.title: ‘Body Language,’ by Meg Howrey
item.description: Meg Howrey’s novel “Body Language” doesn’t skimp on the kind of absurd humor that thrives in a crucible.
item.author: Joumana Khatib

item.title: ‘Profits, Prophets, Coaches, and Kings,’ by Jared Diamond
item.description: In “Profits, Prophets, Coaches, and Kings,” Jared Diamond considers the impact leaders might have had on the course of their civilizations.
item.author: Dan Jones

item.title: ‘The Everest Mystery,’ by Julie Summers and Jochen Hemmleb
item.description: “The Everest Mystery” takes on the enduring puzzle of two climbers’ fates — and pays tribute to the often-overlooked Sandy Irvine.
item.author: W. M. Akers

item.title: ‘American Scoundrel,’ by Kai Bird
item.description: “American Scoundrel” traces the career of Roy Cohn, whose smash-mouth politics continue to shape our own.
item.author: Jennifer Szalai

item.title: ‘53 Days,’ by Timothy W. Ryback
item.description: In “53 Days,” the historian Timothy W. Ryback shows how the Nazis used democratic means to destroy German democracy.
item.author: Sam Adler-Bell

item.title: ‘The Castle,’ by Jon Ronson
item.description: The journalist Jon Ronson finds metaphor and meaning in the story of one man’s baronial fantasia and others like him who are living unmoored from reality.
item.author: Alexandra Jacobs

item.title: ‘The Disappearers,’ by Marlon James
item.description: Marlon James’s story of gay experience and murderous homophobia in Jamaica is a maximalist’s banquet — and the Booker Prize winner’s finest book yet.
item.author: Dwight Garner

item.title: ‘Agrippa,’ by Robert Harris
item.description: Robert Harris’s new novel, “Agrippa,” follows a statesman who witnesses the transformation of a republic into an empire.
item.author: Kathryn Hughes

item.title: ‘Defending the Music,’ by Michael Steinberg
item.description: “The eloquence and depth of his prose remain for me the gold standard,” John Adams writes of Michael Steinberg, who excelled at his craft in the 1960s and ’70s.
item.author: John Adams

item.title: ‘Under Story,’ by Chloe Benjamin
item.description: In “Under Story,” a grieving woman makes a discovery that could help her recover what she thought she had lost forever.
item.author: Lauren LeBlanc

item.title: ‘Hometown,’ by Shaun Tan
item.description: As Shaun Tan reminds us with his stand-alone follow-up to “The Arrival,” some truths are so enormous, so beautiful, they can be told only through myth.
item.author: John Hendrix

item.title: ‘Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea,’ by Emily Wilson
item.description: A new book of essays by the celebrated classicist captures her excitement for her subject matter and the surprising range of her references.
item.author: Jennifer Szalai

item.title: ‘The Black Shield,’ by Wilbert L. Cooper
item.description: In an evocative new memoir, the journalist Wilbert L. Cooper explores the history, and paradoxes, of race and policing in Cleveland, his hometown.
item.author: Eli Saslow

item.title: ‘The Time Tax,’ by Annie Lowrey
item.description: In “The Time Tax,” the Atlantic journalist Annie Lowrey takes aim at bureaucratic red tape.
item.author: Tim Wu

item.title: ‘Heart of Glass,’ by Jennifer Hillier
item.description: In Jennifer Hillier’s new book, a woman must confront her traumatic past after a body washes up on the shores of her seaside town.
item.author: Flynn Berry

item.title: ‘Up on Cove Mountain,’ by Earl Swift
item.description: In “Up on Cove Mountain” Earl Swift confronts a place — and a tragedy — that haunts him.
item.author: Ben McGrath
